title_en: Shandong Jufeng Network Co., Ltd. v. MGAME Company (Korea) and Tianjin Fengyun Network Technology Co., Ltd. — dispute over jurisdiction objection regarding online game agency and license contract
ruling_gist_en: Article 145 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC stipulates: 'The parties to a foreign-related contract may choose the law applicable to the settlement of their contract disputes, unless otherwise provided by law. If the parties to a foreign-related contract do not make a choice, the law of the country that has the closest connection with the contract shall apply.' Article 242 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC stipulates: 'The parties to a dispute arising from a foreign-related contract or from foreign-related property rights and interests may, by written agreement, choose the court of the place that has actual connection with the dispute to exercise jurisdiction. If the people's court of the PRC is chosen to exercise jurisdiction, the provisions of this Law on hierarchical jurisdiction and exclusive jurisdiction shall not be violated.' Article 1 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Foreign-Related Civil or Commercial Contract Dispute Cases stipulates: 'The law applicable to a foreign-related civil or commercial contract refers to the substantive law of the relevant country or region, excluding conflict of laws and procedural law.' Accordingly, the agreement of the parties to a foreign-related contract to choose the applicable law and to choose the court of jurisdiction are two distinct legal acts, and their validity should be determined separately in accordance with relevant legal provisions. The validity of a clause agreeing to choose a court of jurisdiction should be determined in accordance with the lex fori and is irrelevant to the law of the country to which the applicable law belongs. The aforementioned Article 242 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC is an empowering provision rather than a directive provision. That is, under China's current legal provisions, the issue of the parties to a foreign-related contract or foreign-related property rights dispute agreeing to choose a court of jurisdiction must still adhere to the written form requirement and the principle of actual connection.

full_text_en:
Shandong Jufeng Network Co., Ltd. v.

MGAME Corporation (Korea) and Tianjin Fengyun Network

Technology Co., Ltd. — dispute over jurisdiction regarding

online game agency and license contract

Ruling Summary

Article 145 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People’s Republic of China provides: “The parties to a contract involving foreign interests may choose the law applicable to the settlement of their disputes, unless otherwise provided by law. If the parties to a contract involving foreign interests have not made a choice, the law of the country to which the contract is most closely connected shall apply.” Article 242 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People’s Republic of China provides: “The parties to a dispute over a contract involving foreign interests or over property rights and interests involving foreign interests may, by written agreement, choose the court of the place which has actual connection with the dispute to exercise jurisdiction. If the people’s court of the People’s Republic of China is chosen to exercise jurisdiction, the provisions of this Law on jurisdiction by forum level and exclusive jurisdiction shall not be violated.” Article 1 of the Provisions of the Supreme People’s Court on Several Issues concerning the Application of Laws in the Trial of Cases of Disputes over Foreign-related Civil or Commercial Contracts provides: “The law applicable to a foreign-related civil or commercial contract refers to the substantive law of the relevant country or region, and does not include conflict of laws rules and procedural law.” Accordingly, the agreement of the parties to a foreign-related contract to choose the applicable law and the agreement to choose the competent court are two completely different legal acts, and their validity should be determined separately in accordance with the relevant legal provisions. The validity of a clause on agreement to choose the competent court shall be determined in accordance with the law of the forum, and is not related to the legal provisions of the country to which the lex causae belongs. The aforementioned Article 242 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People’s Republic of China is an authorization norm, not a directive norm. That is, according to the current legal provisions of our country, for the issue of the parties to a dispute over a foreign-related contract or foreign-related property rights and interests agreeing to choose the competent court, the principles of written form and actual connection must still be adhered to.

Civil Ruling of the Supreme People’s Court

(2009) Min San Zhong Zi No. 4

Appellant (Defendant at First Instance): MGAME CORPORATION (Korea), domiciled at JEI Platz 8, 459-11, Gasan-dong, Geumcheon-gu, Seoul, 153-803, the Republic of Korea.

Legal Representative: Kweon Yi Hyung, Chief Executive Officer.

Agent ad litem: Wang Yaxi, lawyer of Beijing King & Wood Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: He Wei, lawyer of Beijing King & Wood Law Firm.

Appellee (Plaintiff at First Instance): Shandong Jufeng Network Co., Ltd., domiciled at Room 1102, 11th Floor, Building B, Sanqing Century Fortune Center, No. 359 Xinyu Road, High-tech Zone, Jinan City, Shandong Province, People’s Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Liu Guanjin, Chairman of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Tian Jueci, Deputy General Manager of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Lu Guangzhou, Deputy General Manager of the Company.

Third Party at First Instance: Tianjin Fengyun Network Technology Co., Ltd., domiciled at Haitai Torch Park, No. 2 Wuhua Road, Nankai District, Tianjin, People’s Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Bao Jiandong, Chairman of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Ren Yanli, Administrative Director of the Company.

In the case of the dispute over jurisdiction regarding the online game agency and license contract between the plaintiff at first instance, Shandong Jufeng Network Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Jufeng Network Company), and the defendant at first instance, MGAME CORPORATION (Korea) (hereinafter referred to as MGAME Company), and the third party at first instance, Tianjin Fengyun Network Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Fengyun Network Company), MGAME Company appealed against the civil ruling (2008) Lu Min San Chu Zi No. 1 rendered by the Shandong High People’s Court of the People’s Republic of China on January 12, 2009, to this Court. This Court formed a collegial panel according to law and held a public hearing on March 25, 2009. The agent ad litem of the appellant MGAME Company, Wang Yaxi and He Wei, the agent ad litem of the appellee Jufeng Network Company, Tian Jueci and Lu Guangzhou, and the agent ad litem of the third party at first instance, Fengyun Network Company, Ren Yanli, appeared in court to participate in the proceedings. During the hearing, none of the parties applied for withdrawal. The case is now concluded.

On July 30, 2008, Jufeng Network Company filed a lawsuit with the Shandong High People’s Court, naming MGAME Company as the defendant and Fengyun Network Company as the third party, requesting a judgment: 1. that the defendant continue to perform the “Exclusive Game Agency and License Agreement” signed by both parties on March 10, 2005; 2. that the defendant compensate the plaintiff for economic losses in the amount of RMB 3,349,827,241; and 3. that the defendant bear all litigation costs of this case.

After the Shandong High People’s Court accepted the case, the defendant MGAME Company raised an objection to the jurisdiction within the period for submitting the statement of defense. Its main reason was: Article 21 of the “Game License Agreement” signed by the plaintiff and defendant on March 25, 2005 stipulated: “This Agreement shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of China. All disputes arising out of or in connection with this Agreement shall be finally settled in Singapore, and all disputes arising out of this Agreement shall be subject to the jurisdiction of Singapore.” Therefore, submitting disputes arising from this Agreement to the judicial authorities of Singapore for jurisdiction was the explicit agreement of both parties and the true expression of their intent. This case should be tried by a competent court in Singapore. The Shandong High People’s Court has no jurisdiction over this case. Therefore, it requested that the lawsuit of Jufeng Network Company be dismissed.

Upon examination, the Shandong High People’s Court held that: This case is a foreign-related intellectual property dispute. Although Article 21 of the “Game License Agreement” signed by the plaintiff Jufeng Network Company and the defendant MGAME Company on March 25, 2005 stipulated that disputes arising therefrom should be subject to the jurisdiction of Singapore, the parties also stipulated at the same time that “this Agreement shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of China.” The parties chose the law of China as the lex causae for the applicable law of the agreement. Therefore, the agreement on jurisdiction clause of the parties must also comply with the relevant provisions of the chosen lex causae, i.e., Chinese law. Article 242 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People’s Republic of China provides: “The parties to a dispute over a contract involving foreign interests or over property rights and interests involving foreign interests may, by written agreement, choose the court of the place which has actual connection with the dispute to exercise jurisdiction. ...” Accordingly, the court chosen by the parties should be limited to the place which has actual connection with the disputed case. In this case, the place of jurisdiction agreed upon by Jufeng Network Company and MGAME Company, Singapore, is neither the domicile of either party, nor the place of signing, place of performance, or place where the dispute arose of this game license agreement. Therefore, it has no connection whatsoever with the dispute in this case. The agreement exceeded the limitation of actual connection with the dispute, and this agreed jurisdiction should be invalid. The Shandong High People’s Court, as the court of the domicile of the plaintiff Jufeng Network Company, has actual connection with this case. Under the circumstance that the agreed jurisdiction clause is invalid, it is not improper for the Shandong High People’s Court to exercise jurisdiction over this case, which complies with the legal provisions of our country. Pursuant to Article 38 and Article 242 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People’s Republic of China, the Shandong High People’s Court ruled: The objection to jurisdiction raised by MGAME CORPORATION (Korea) in this case is dismissed. The case acceptance fee of RMB 50 yuan shall be borne by MGAME CORPORATION (Korea).

MGAME Company disagreed with the original ruling and appealed to this Court, requesting that the original ruling be revoked, the lawsuit of Jufeng Network Company be dismissed, and the case acceptance fees for the first and second instances be borne by Jufeng Network Company. Its main reasons were: 1. The original ruling violated legal procedures. On November 14, 2008, the court of first instance served on MGAME Company case materials that only included Jufeng Network Company’s statement of claims and facts and reasons, without any supporting evidence. To protect its procedural rights, MGAME Company could only raise the jurisdiction objection based on the evidence it already possessed. The court of first instance failed to serve on MGAME Company the complete complaint materials, violating the provisions of Article 110 and Article 246 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People’s Republic of China, depriving MGAME Company of the right to debate the claims and evidence of Jufeng Network Company in the jurisdiction objection proceedings. Its ruling seriously violated legal procedures and should be revoked according to law. 2. The original ruling had unclear findings of facts. In the “Facts and Reasons” section of its complaint, Jufeng Network Company claimed that “the plaintiff and defendant signed an ‘Exclusive Game Agency and License Agreement’ for the internet game ‘Hero’ on March 10, 2005,” and “the validity period of the contract was from March 10, 2005 to March 1, 2008.” The evidence attached by MGAME Company when submitting its “Objection to Jurisdiction” to the court of first instance was the “Exclusive Game Distribution and License Agreement” signed by MGAME Company and Jufeng Network Company on March 25, 2005, with a term of two years. The above two agreements are not the same agreement. MGAME Company has not signed the agreement provided by Jufeng Network Company, and because it did not receive the agreement, MGAME Company could not determine whether it had signed the agreement or what the jurisdiction clause therein stipulated. The court of first instance did not examine the agreement submitted by Jufeng Network Company at the time of filing the lawsuit, but instead relied on the relevant clauses of the March 25, 2008 agreement submitted by MGAME Company to determine that the agreed jurisdiction between Jufeng Network Company and MGAME Company was invalid, thereby dismissing MGAME Company’s objection to jurisdiction in this case, which constitutes unclear findings of facts. 3. According to the agreement in the “Exclusive Game Distribution and License Agreement” signed by MGAME Company and Jufeng Network Company on March 25, 2005, all disputes arising from this agreement should be under the jurisdiction of the courts of Singapore. During the process of concluding the agreement, MGAME Company and Jufeng Network Company repeatedly negotiated the matters concerning the jurisdiction clause. Jufeng Network Company advocated for jurisdiction by the Chinese court of its domicile, while MGAME Company advocated for jurisdiction by the Korean court of its domicile. Ultimately, both parties reached a compromise and decided that the judicial authorities of a third country should have jurisdiction, which is the content of Article 21 of the agreement. The original intention of this agreement was to avoid any unfair handling of disputes related to the agreement that might arise due to national or local protectionism. Having the court of first instance hear the disputes arising from this agreement clearly violates the true intention of the parties and is also unfair to MGAME Company. The court of first instance has no jurisdiction over this case.

Jufeng Network Company argued in defense that the original ruling had clear findings of facts and correct application of law, and should be affirmed according to law. Its main reasons were: 1. The original ruling complied with legal procedures. The license agreement signed by both parties on March 25, 2005 explicitly stipulated that “this Agreement is governed by Chinese law and construed in accordance with Chinese law.” Although it was agreed that disputes should be under the jurisdiction of the judicial authorities of Singapore, because it did not comply with the requirement of “actual connection with the dispute” under Chinese law, it was an invalid agreement. 2. The original ruling had clear findings of facts and correct application of law. The validity period of the “Exclusive Game Agency and License Agreement” signed by both parties on March 25, 2005 was from March 2005 to March 2008. This was the validity period of the contract, not the statute of limitations. This does not affect the place of jurisdiction for disputes between the parties. 3. At the time of signing the agreement, there were two versions, Chinese and English. The English version was dated March 25, and the Chinese version was dated March 10. Both were components of the contract with identical content.

The third party at first instance, Fengyun Network Company, did not state any opinion.

Upon trial, this Court finds: In the “Civil Complaint” filed by Jufeng Network Company, the Facts and Reasons section stated: “The plaintiff and defendant signed an ‘Exclusive Game Agency and License Agreement’ for the internet game ‘Hero’ on March 10, 2005.” After filing the lawsuit but before the court accepted the case, Jufeng Network Company also submitted corresponding evidentiary materials to the court. Item 1 of its “Evidence List” was described as “Chinese and English versions of the ‘Online Game License Agreement’ signed by the plaintiff and defendant on March 10, 2005.” However, the Chinese text contract copy attached as evidence had a front page with a signing date of “March 25, 2005,” a front page contract name of “Online Game License Agreement” and “Game Name: ‘Hero Online’”, and a second page contract name of “Exclusive Game Agency and License Agreement.” This Chinese text contract had no signatures or seals. The English text contract copy attached as evidence had a front page with a signing date of “March 25, 2005,” a front page contract name of “GAME LICENSE AGREEMENT” and “Hero Online Game Hero Online,” and a second page contract name of “Exclusive Game Distribution and License Agreement.” Each page of this English text contract bore the signatures of the representatives of the appellant and the appellee, and the front page bore the copyright registration seal of the Shandong Provincial Copyright Bureau. During the second instance hearing, Jufeng Network Company submitted to this Court a Chinese text with a front page signing date of “March 10, 2005,” a front page contract name of “Online Game License Agreement” and “Game Name: ‘Hero Online’”, and a second page contract name of “Exclusive Game Agency and License Agreement.” The contract signing page (page 13) bore the official seals and signatures of the representatives of the appellant and the appellee. During the second instance hearing, MGAME Company submitted to this Court a Chinese text translated by China Translation & Publishing Corporation from the English text original of the contract, which was identical in content to the English text copy submitted by Jufeng Network Company at the time of filing the lawsuit in the first instance. Each page of the English text and the contract bore the signatures of the representatives of the appellant and the appellee. The signing representatives in each version were the same, but the signatures were slightly different. During the second instance hearing, both the appellant and the appellee explicitly recognized the authenticity of the English text of the Game License Agreement dated March 25, 2005, and confirmed that there was no other transaction contract between the parties. As for the Chinese text agreement with a front page date of March 10, 2005 submitted by Jufeng Network Company in the second instance, MGAME Company argued that it had never signed this agreement with the appellee and that there were many content differences compared to the Game License Agreement dated March 25, 2005, which both parties recognized. Therefore, it did not acknowledge the authenticity of this evidence.

According to the Chinese text of the March 25, 2005 agreement translated by China Translation & Publishing Corporation provided by MGAME Company, the preamble states: “The agreement content is that Jufeng Network Co., Ltd. becomes the exclusive game distributor of the Licensor (referring to MGAME Company) and promotes the Products in the Designated Territory in accordance with the following terms and conditions (each term is defined below) ... ‘Designated Territory’ refers exclusively to mainland China (excluding Hong Kong)”; Article 6.1 stipulates: “The Licensor will provide technical services related to the installation and maintenance of the Items at the premises of the Licensee (referring to Jufeng Network Company) during the Agreement term ...”; Article 21 states: “This Agreement shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of China. All disputes arising out of or in connection with this Agreement shall be finally settled in Singapore, and all disputes arising out of this Agreement shall be subject to the jurisdiction of Singapore.” Upon verification by this Court, the English texts of the Game License Agreement dated March 25, 2005 submitted by both parties are completely consistent in the English expressions of at least the preamble, Article 6.1, and Article 21.

It is further found that the Shandong High People’s Court received Jufeng Network Company’s “Civil Complaint” on July 30, 2008, received two volumes of evidentiary materials provided by Jufeng Network Company on August 17, 2008, and decided to accept the case on August 21, 2008. Thereafter, the court served on MGAME Company the notice of responding to the lawsuit, a copy of the complaint, a notice of burden of proof, and a summons for hearing, but did not serve the evidentiary materials submitted by Jufeng Network Company at the same time.

This Court holds that the main issues disputed by the parties in the second instance are: the authenticity of the agreement on which Jufeng Network Company’s lawsuit is based; whether the court of first instance’s failure to serve the plaintiff’s submitted evidentiary materials simultaneously with the service of the copy of the complaint violates legal procedures; whether the clause in the contract on agreement to choose the competent court is valid; and whether the court of first instance has jurisdiction over this case.

(1) Concerning the authenticity of the agreement on which Jufeng Network Company’s lawsuit is based

Although Jufeng Network Company stated in its complaint that the agreement signed with MGAME Company was the “Exclusive Game Agency and License Agreement” dated March 10, 2005, and even described it in its “Evidence List” as “Chinese and English versions of the ‘Online Game License Agreement’ signed by the plaintiff and defendant on March 10, 2005,” the evidentiary materials it actually submitted with the complaint were the English text of the agreement dated March 25, 2005, signed by both parties, and an unsigned Chinese text dated the same day. This English text is the same agreement as the English text of the agreement on which MGAME Company based its objection to jurisdiction. Both Jufeng Network Company and MGAME Company explicitly recognized the authenticity of this English text during the second instance hearing, and both confirmed that there was no other transaction contract between the parties. Consequently, regardless of the authenticity of the Chinese text of the “Online Game License Agreement” submitted by Jufeng Network Company in the second instance, which has a front page date of March 10, 2005 and bears the official seals and representative signatures of the appellant and the appellee at the contract execution page, this does not affect the parties’ litigation based on the English text of the agreement dated March 25, 2005. Because Jufeng Network Company failed to accurately and clearly state the signing date of the agreement between the parties in its complaint due to its own reasons, this may have caused some confusion for MGAME Company in responding to the lawsuit. However, given that the agreement actually relied upon by both parties refers to the March 25, 2005 agreement, and the court of first instance also ruled on MGAME Company’s objection to jurisdiction based on this agreement, the issue of the agreement date description did not substantially impede MGAME Company’s exercise of its litigation rights. Therefore, the appellant’s argument that the original ruling had unclear findings of facts on this point is actually not valid.

(2) Whether the court of first instance’s failure to simultaneously serve the plaintiff’s submitted evidentiary materials when serving the copy of the complaint violates legal procedures

Article 113, paragraph 1 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "The people's court shall, within five days from the date of filing the case, send a copy of the bill of complaint to the defendant, and the defendant shall, within fifteen days from the date of receipt, submit a statement of defense." Article 33 of the Several Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence in Civil Proceedings (hereinafter referred to as the Evidence Provisions) provides: "When serving the notice of acceptance of the case and the notice of response to the lawsuit, the people's court shall at the same time serve the notice on evidence production on the parties. The notice on evidence production shall specify the principles and requirements for the allocation of the burden of proof, the circumstances under which a party may apply to the people's court for investigation and collection of evidence, the time limit for evidence production designated by the people's court in light of the circumstances of the case, and the legal consequences of failing to provide evidence within the time limit. The time limit for evidence production may be agreed upon by the parties through consultation and confirmed by the people's court. Where the people's court designates the time limit for evidence production, the designated time limit shall be not less than thirty days, calculated from the day following the date on which the parties receive the notice of acceptance of the case and the notice of response to the lawsuit." Article 34, paragraph 1 of the Evidence Provisions provides: "The parties shall submit evidentiary materials to the people's court within the time limit for evidence production; if a party fails to submit evidence within the time limit for evidence production, it shall be deemed to have waived the right to produce evidence." Article 37 of the Evidence Provisions provides: "Upon a party's application, the people's court may organize the parties to exchange evidence before the court session. For cases involving voluminous evidence or complex and difficult issues, the people's court shall organize the parties to exchange evidence after the expiration of the defense period and before the court session."

According to the above legal provisions, first, the people's court shall, within five days from the date of filing the case, serve at least the copy of the bill of complaint, the notice of response to the lawsuit, and the notice on evidence production on the defendant. There is no mandatory provision requiring that the plaintiff's evidence be served on the defendant simultaneously. Second, the aforementioned judicial interpretation clarifies the system of the time limit for evidence production after the people's court accepts and files the case. That is, unless the parties reach an agreement through consultation and the people's court confirms it, the time limit for evidence production shall be calculated from the day following the date on which the parties receive the notice of acceptance of the case and the notice of response to the lawsuit and shall be not less than thirty days. For domestic cases, this time limit for evidence production is clearly longer than the defendant's fifteen-day defense period; even for defendants in foreign-related cases who have no domicile within the territory of the People's Republic of China, their defense period is thirty days, and the time limit for evidence production can only possibly be the same as the defense period, but will not be shorter than the defense period, and in practice is generally longer than the defense period. Although in practice, when the people's court decides to accept and file a case, it generally requires the plaintiff to provide preliminary evidence, this does not mean that the plaintiff must submit all evidence at the time of filing the lawsuit or before the expiration of the defendant's defense period. Third, the aforementioned judicial interpretation also clarifies the system of evidence exchange, which means that the parties may provide evidence to each other when the people's court organizes the exchange of evidence, and there is no requirement that the plaintiff's evidence must be served on the defendant in advance. In addition, how to ensure that the defendant obtains the plaintiff's evidence as early as possible to enable it to conduct targeted defenses in a timely manner is an issue that needs further improvement of relevant legal rules and practices in the future. In summary, the appellant's ground of appeal that the court of first instance violated legal procedures by failing to serve the plaintiff's evidence simultaneously with the service of the copy of the bill of complaint cannot be sustained.

(III) Regarding the validity of the clause on the choice of court agreement in the contract involved

Article 145 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "Parties to a contract involving foreign interests may choose the law applicable to the settlement of their contractual disputes, except as otherwise provided by law. If parties to a contract involving foreign interests have not made a choice, the law of the country having the closest connection with the contract shall apply." Article 242 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "Parties to a dispute over a contract involving foreign interests or over property rights and interests involving foreign interests may, by written agreement, choose the court of a place that has actual connection with the dispute as the court of jurisdiction. If a people's court of the People's Republic of China is chosen to exercise jurisdiction, the provisions of this Law regarding hierarchical jurisdiction and exclusive jurisdiction shall not be violated." Article 1 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Disputes over Foreign-Related Civil or Commercial Contracts provides: "The law applicable to a foreign-related civil or commercial contract refers to the substantive law of the relevant country or region, excluding conflict of laws rules and procedural law." According to the above legal provisions, the choice of applicable law by agreement and the choice of court by agreement are two completely different legal acts, and their validity should be determined separately according to relevant legal provisions. The validity of a clause on the choice of court by agreement should be determined according to the law of the forum country; the reasoning of the court of first instance in its ruling that the clause on the choice of court by agreement must comply with the relevant legal provisions of the country to which the chosen applicable law belongs is erroneous.

Regarding the issue of parties to foreign-related cases choosing a court by agreement, the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (for Trial Implementation), which came into effect on October 1, 1982, did not contain specific provisions. The current Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, promulgated and implemented on April 9, 1991, includes the above specific provision in Article 242. According to the legislative background and relevant legislative intent at the time, the provision that "by written agreement, choose the court of a place that has actual connection with the dispute as the court of jurisdiction" in this article should be understood as an authorizing norm, not a directive norm. That is, when parties to a dispute over a contract involving foreign interests or over property rights and interests involving foreign interests choose a court by agreement, they should choose a court of a place that has actual connection with the dispute; otherwise, the choice of court agreement is invalid. At the same time, such an agreement on the choice of court may be either agreed in advance or agreed afterwards, but must be fixed and confirmed in some written form. Accordingly, under the current laws of China, the principles of written form and actual connection should still be adhered to for the issue of parties to a dispute over a contract involving foreign interests or over property rights and interests involving foreign interests choosing a court by agreement.

In this case, according to the English version of the contract unanimously recognized by the appellant and the appellee, Clause 21 stipulates two basic aspects. That is, first, it stipulates the substantive law applicable to disputes arising from the agreement, namely Chinese law; and then, it stipulates the dispute resolution body for disputes arising from the agreement, namely subjecting to the jurisdiction of Singapore. The appellant and the appellee only dispute the validity of the clause on choosing a foreign judicial body's jurisdiction by agreement in this case. According to the above legal provisions, especially Article 242 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, parties to a foreign-related contract choosing a court by agreement should choose a court of a place that has actual connection with the dispute. However, Singapore, which the parties in this case agreed to refer to, is neither the domicile of the parties, nor the place of performance of the contract, the place of signing of the contract, or the location of the subject matter. At the same time, the law chosen by the parties in this case is not Singapore law, and the appellant also failed to prove that Singapore has any other actual connection with the dispute in this case. Therefore, it should be considered that Singapore has no actual connection with the dispute in this case. Accordingly, the agreement on dispute jurisdiction in Clause 21 of the contract involved should be deemed invalid and cannot serve as the basis for determining the jurisdiction of this case. The appellant's claims on the issue of dispute jurisdiction based on this agreement cannot be supported. The ruling of the court of first instance, which considered the place where the dispute arose as one of the connecting points for determining whether it is a place with actual connection with the dispute within the meaning of Article 242 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, although improper, does not affect the determination of the validity of the agreement on dispute jurisdiction in Clause 21 of the contract involved.

(IV) Regarding the basis for the court of first instance to exercise jurisdiction over this case

Where the agreement of the parties on the choice of court is invalid, the jurisdiction of the case shall be determined according to other legal rules on jurisdiction of foreign-related cases of the country where the court is situated. Article 241 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "An action arising from a contract dispute or other disputes over property rights and interests brought against a defendant who has no domicile within the territory of the People's Republic of China, if the contract is signed or performed within the territory of the People's Republic of China, or the subject matter of the action is located within the territory of the People's Republic of China, or the defendant has property within the territory of the People's Republic of China that can be attached, or the defendant has a representative office within the territory of the People's Republic of China, may be filed with the people's court of the place where the contract is signed, the place where the contract is performed, the place where the subject matter of the action is located, the place where the property that can be attached is located, the place where the tortious act is committed, or the place where the representative office is located."

In this case, according to the English version of the contract unanimously recognized by the appellant and the appellee, the territorial scope of the license of rights under the contract, i.e., the "designated territory," refers specifically to "Mainland China." Thus, it can be seen that the contract in dispute is performed within the territory of the People's Republic of China. Although the contract does not explicitly stipulate the specific places for performing most of the contractual obligations within the territory of the People's Republic of China, the place of performance of some contractual obligations is clear, such as in Article 6.1, where the place for MGAME to perform its technical service obligations is explicitly stipulated as the premises of Jufeng Network Company. Under such circumstances, it should be considered that Shandong Province, where Jufeng Network Company is located, is also the place of performance of the contract. Accordingly, the Shandong High People's Court, as the court of the place of performance of the contract in this case, has jurisdiction over this case. The ruling of the court of first instance, which found that the Shandong High People's Court, as the court of the domicile of the plaintiff Jufeng Network Company, had actual connection with this case and therefore had jurisdiction over this case, although its reasoning was improper, the result is not erroneous.

In summary, the grounds of appeal of the appellant MGAME Company, that the court of first instance violated legal procedures, found unclear facts, and that this case should be under the jurisdiction of a Singapore court, cannot be sustained. Although some expressions in the reasoning of the ruling of the court of first instance are inappropriate, the result of its ruling is not erroneous, and its application of law is basically correct. Pursuant to Article 153, paragraph 1, item (1) and Article 154 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the ruling is as follows: The appeal is dismissed and the original ruling is affirmed.

This ruling is final.
